hlni.insight: A degree title does not define assessment methods; auditing specific task criteria does.
hlni.audienceGap: Students assume degree names inherently describe the type of work they will perform.
hlni.viewerChange: Students will now ask 'How is this assessed?' rather than relying on degree labels.
hlni.support: The three-column audit separates product, criteria, and feedback, allowing students to verify actual course expectations.
hlni.payoff: The method identifies specific knowledge gaps that the student must investigate to make an informed decision.

reelTitle: B.Com vs BBA: The Assessment Audit
creativeAngle: Moving beyond degree titles by auditing specific assessment methods.
objective: Build credibility by teaching a practical method to compare degree requirements.
targetAudience: +2 students seeking academic depth and well-supported course and career decisions

shots.name: The Dilemma
shots.visual: Student holds a sheet labelled 'Assessment Audit' with two blank columns: B.Com and BBA.
shots.dialogue: Choosing between B.Com and BBA? Don't guess. Audit the assessment.

shots.name: The Method
shots.visual: Student fills in three rows: 'Product', 'Criteria', and 'Feedback' for a sample subject.
shots.dialogue: List the expected product, assessment criteria, and available feedback. If criteria are missing, that is your question.
shots.cameraPerformance: Top-down view of the hand writing.

shots.name: The Payoff
shots.visual: Student taps the empty cell on the page, looking directly at the camera.
shots.dialogue: Titles aren't enough. Use these gaps to ask how you will actually be evaluated.

productionNotes.camera: Stable, clear focus on the document.
productionNotes.editing: Steady cuts between the student and the audit sheet.

creativeSummary.keyCreativeIdea: Transforming a vague degree comparison into a concrete audit of assessment tasks.

selected.title: The Assessment Audit
selected.audienceGap: Students assume the degree name tells them how they will be evaluated.
selected.hlni: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive. Ask these as separate questions.
selected.viewerChange: Learns to look past degree titles to check specific assessment criteria.
selected.concept: A student holds a blank 'Assessment Audit' worksheet and breaks down a sample assignment into three columns: Product, Criteria, and Feedback.
selected.device: Direct address to camera using the worksheet to show that 'Marketing' or 'Accounting' tasks can have vastly different assessment criteria.
selected.support: The method separates three different pieces of information; it does not assume particular course content.
methodSteps: Ask what criterion is used to assess it.
Ask what feedback is available; mark unknown answers as questions.
selected.interpretationRule: Use the unanswered cells to ask a precise question about the actual course or task before deciding.
selected.visibleProof: A three-column question sheet turns one vague preference into a concrete unanswered question.
selected.payoff: Use the unanswered cells to ask a precise question about the actual course or task before deciding.
selected.limitations: This is a question-forming aid, not a degree ranking, aptitude test or prediction of success.

comparedWith.hlni: A task label alone does not tell you what you must produce, what will be assessed, or what feedback you receive. Ask these as separate questions.
comparedWith.device: Direct address to camera using the worksheet to show that 'Marketing' or 'Accounting' tasks can have vastly different assessment criteria.

comparedWith.hlni: A short illustrative activity can reveal where you need help or what you want to investigate next; it cannot determine which degree suits you.
comparedWith.device: Natural conversation showing that being 'stuck' on a specific detail is a productive starting point for a better question.

comparedWith.hlni: The same total can result from different component values; an aggregate alone cannot tell you the underlying mix.
comparedWith.device: A sliding scale animation showing how 100 credits can be divided differently, challenging the viewer to ask for the breakdown.

conceptSelection.contrast: Trust uses a structural auditing tool to build credibility; Connection uses a personal journaling process to normalize inquiry; Discovery uses a mathematical counterexample to challenge assumptions about degree equivalence.
